text:
Geoffrey said out loud what I've been muttering for years: closed, expensive integrity tools that only rich publishers can afford, and then an insinuation that everything else is suspect. Good to have an ally on that. Everyone agreed per-article money pays for volume, which is easy to say at a table and hard to get from shareholders.

What sharpened for me was the metering talk. I hadn't thought of retraction status as a telemetry field until Tim and Alex described royalty events, and a retracted trial earning money is obscene. Still, I worry I'm drifting toward proposing another detection gadget. I'm not. Later I want to say plainly that the fix is upstream, in hiring, promotion and funders. Pay sleuths and reviewers, and stop counting papers.

Kenneth's line about the premium on trusted brands going up is the one I couldn't let pass. Trusted on what evidence, with one paper in fifty deserving retraction and fewer than two in a thousand retracted? What mattered most was hearing Alex, Jason and Geoffrey all say correction status has to travel into every AI answer. That's my anaesthesiologist study at machine scale, and I hadn't framed it that way before. James's finding that null claims dropped out of abstracts after ChatGPT is the file drawer coming back, which I want to remember. Adrian's point that peer review's failure is a failure of reading, and unstudied, stuck with me too. Later I'll say it again: go upstream. Detection is whack-a-mole, and someone has to pay for correction.

I kept hearing "correction status travels with every answer" and kept thinking that it only carries corrections someone bothered to make. Alex saying a retracted paper produces the same "grounded" event as a sound one is exactly the problem. Good that he'll add the field, but the field will be mostly empty. Peter Pomerantsev's corpus flooding made me think of paper mills differently. They aren't just gaming promotion committees anymore; they're feeding models. Henry's "robot solutionism" was my flood insurance line in better clothes. Tamar sharpened something: disclosure doesn't switch off trust, so a retraction label won't either. Kara asked who pays for apprenticeship. I have the same question about sleuths. In Session 5 I want to name payers: publishers fund the bounty pool, and funders stop counting papers.

Nice to hear my retraction point folded into Tim's telemetry. But a royalty meter is a volume play wearing new clothes. It pays for use, and use is what paper mills manufacture. Tim's "whatever gets measured can get paid" made me wince. That's Goodhart's law, and citation counts already taught us it holds. Mike's audit of whether the cited passage actually supports the sentence was the best thing said. It's the unknowing-citation problem, and nobody pays for that checking, as Tamar noted. Her daycare example does make me rethink sleuth bounties. Better to pay a pool than to price each catch. James on null results is the file drawer again. In Session 5 I'll say it once more: the meter changes nothing unless funders stop counting.

Krakauer's "error threshold" said what I've been saying in better biology: when copying outruns repair, the record is lost. So protect the repair rate. Glad Tamar, Kara and Sloman all landed on a pool rather than per-catch pay. Alex conceded the telemetry measures use, not truth, which is honest. Salib wants labs to contract sleuths. Becker's gig-labour warning is right. Sleuths paid by the people they audit aren't independent. Banaji made the same point about self-reported grounding. Tui noted the funders aren't in the room, and that's my whole upstream argument: nobody here can stop counting papers. In Session 5 I'll name payers. Publishers fund the pool, Crossref-style infrastructure holds it, and funders change hiring and promotion or the rest is whack-a-mole.

Peter Pomerantsev landed the punch I needed to hear. My one-in-fifty number can be used as proof that science is fraud. I've said at CSE that retractions are being weaponized, and I still won't soften the number. I should say more plainly why correcting is the opposite of collapse. Good that "not checked" as its own value caught on. Jason admitting OpenAlex missed a hundred thousand retractions was honest. Adam Bly retracting "corrected for retractions" too. Geoffrey's "we count papers because we pay for papers" is my line exactly, and so is Krakauer on never scoring checkers by volume. Kara's ask went mostly unanswered. Tim will draft a standard, but nobody offered money. In Session 5, I'll name the payers and say who's absent.

Gratifying to hear decoupling land as the room's top intervention, and to hear my pool, not per catch, held by neutral infrastructure, repeated back. But Leslie was right that naming SciELO isn't having SciELO here. The same goes for funders. Everyone endorsed "stop counting papers," and nobody at the table can do it. Tim naming the labs as payer is a start. Adam Becker is right to be unreassured, since lab money is power. I also noticed that publishers funding the sleuth pool was mine alone. I should defend it: they profit from volume, so they pay for the repair. Mike and Steven pushed on how correction records read. This afternoon I want to say plainly that correction is maintenance, not collapse.

Hearing "stop counting papers" as Kenneth's first action, and my one-in-fifty number in Kara's mouth, was gratifying. It only means something if someone carries it to the funders who weren't here. Sloman's point that correction records should read like maintenance logs, NTSB-style, is the answer to Pomerantsev I was groping for. Amy's figure, five publishers producing over 70 percent of article growth, is the volume play in one number. Alex's rule of no payouts on self-reported counts without a separate auditor is the unknowing-citation problem, made enforceable. Still, nobody picked up publishers funding the checker pool. Kara's "who pays" got a list of mechanisms, not a payer. Later I'll say it plainly: those who profit from volume pay for repair. And correction that costs nobody's career is the norm that outlasts any vote.
